cells.tense: You're here at the open door with your hand on it, and you're closing it on purpose.
cells.verb: Letting go of what's finished, deliberately, like setting down a tool you've stopped needing.
cells.place: Standing at the end of something that has genuinely ended — the room after the last box is out.
cells.ask: Offer the next small thing some care before it has to earn it: water it while it's barely sprouting, tend one new thing for a week without checking whether it's working, and what comes back is growth that happens on its own — the kind that doesn't leave you wrung out.
cells.core: You're letting go of something finished, and you're doing it with your hands open. That's not losing it — the thing has run its course and you can feel that it has, so the releasing isn't grief, it's the relief that comes after. There's a kind of quiet in you that only arrives when a person stops gripping, and you're standing in it. What you've carried so long is lighter, and the lightness is its own reward.
cells.sheetLine: You let go of what was done, and the letting go felt like arrival.

cells.tense: You're bracing for an ending that hasn't arrived — already packed, already practiced the goodbye.
cells.verb: Letting go early, before the thing is done, and making a show of the surrender.
cells.place: Standing at a door that's still open, rehearsing the walk through it, giving away what you could still use.
cells.ask: Bring one small practice to this — a thing you do at the same time each day, a steady light you keep without needing it to fix anything — and what comes back is a steadiness that connects instead of isolates, refinement that serves you instead of feeding the panic: practice flows without force.
cells.core: You're already letting go of something that hasn't finished. You can feel the ending coming and you've jumped ahead of it, clearing space before the thing is actually over, and somewhere under that there's a kind of self-denial at work — handing over what you still need, calling it surrender before it's surrender. The bracing costs you the thing you're trying to hold. You're not letting go — you're flinching forward.
cells.sheetLine: You're giving up before the ending has come, and calling it surrender.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that closed behind you — your hand is on the handle of a room you're not in anymore.
cells.verb: Holding on, gripping what's already gone, refusing the release because the grip has become the thing you do.
cells.place: At the edge of an ending you never completed, still carrying what could be set down, tired in a way sleep doesn't touch.
cells.ask: Let something steady hold you for a while — one person, one routine, one structure that can bear your weight without asking you to be stronger than you are — and what comes back is a capacity that contains rather than crushes: holding without forcing.
cells.core: You're holding something that has already ended. It's not that you don't know — it's that the holding has become the thing you do, and it's exhausting now in a way it wasn't when the thing was alive. You've been carrying this so long that setting it down feels like the ground would tilt. The release isn't coming because the ending never finished. You're tired in the part of you that keeps holding.
cells.sheetLine: You're still gripping what ended, and the grip is wearing you down.

cells.tense: The pen is already down and the page is already written, and you're reading it as someone else's hand.
cells.verb: Releasing what's done without knowing you're the one who released it — or telling yourself you haven't let go when you already have.
cells.place: In the room after the ending, standing among the cleared shelves, saying you're still in the middle of it.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're tending and admit you're tending it — say out loud that this is care, not logistics — and what comes back is growth without forcing, a space you're holding that doesn't need you to clutch it.
cells.core: You've already let go of something — you can feel it in how you talk about the thing, in the past tense you keep slipping into — and you're still describing yourself as someone who hasn't. Or the other way: you're telling yourself you surrendered when the truth is you're still holding, and the grip has gone unnoticed. The release is happening or it isn't, and either way you're not claiming it. The letting go is running under your feet; the saying-so hasn't caught up.
cells.sheetLine: You've already surrendered, or you haven't — and you're not saying which.

flags.detail: "a while ago" — a cell knows no one's past
